video_title: 36% of Your Portfolio Just Disappeared In the Last 30 Years (Andrew Ang Explains How)
gist: Columbia professor Andrew Ang (Tao Balance, ex-BlackRock factor head) describes AI agent swarms that specialize, vote and self-improve to replace parts of the investment committee, and his multi-layer factor framework behind the SEI ETF ANGU. His 'Uncle Sam's Cut' paper shows federal taxes cost US equity investors ~160-170 bps a year (about 36% of wealth over 30 years), a historically low drag he expects to rise, making private credit and yield products far less attractive after tax.

themes.theme: Agentic swarms replacing the investment committee

insights.claim: Andrew Ang's 'self-driving portfolio' uses AI agents for three advantages over human teams: scale (parallel specialization), interaction (agents critique and vote on each other's proposals), and continuous learning.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Agentic asset allocation is a workflow redesign, not task substitution.

insights.claim: Rather than relying on a single mean-variance optimizer, Ang runs dozens of agents each specializing in one portfolio construction method, from market-cap and equal weight to hierarchical risk parity and total portfolio approaches.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Model diversification at the portfolio-construction layer reduces single-method risk.

insights.claim: Ang argues the most valuable signal from agent swarms is 'productive dissent': agents can disagree without the HR conflicts or talent departures that make disagreement costly in human teams, and the best opportunities are where disagreement is highest.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Disagreement among agents can be harvested as an information signal for opportunity selection.
insights.quote: the best opportunities are the ones where there is a lot of disagreement

insights.claim: Agents are evaluated not just on whether returns were higher but on reasoning quality, e.g. whether their expected-return forecast and rationale matched realized fundamentals, and a meta-agent orchestrates a self-improvement cycle with guardrails on which code and skills may change.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Process-level evaluation and logged, ratifiable changes make self-modifying agents auditable.

insights.claim: Under a tight investment policy statement (long-only, low-cost ETFs, factor-exposure limits, bounded deviations from a 60/40 target), Ang says agent-built portfolios do not look very different from human ones, and a radically different output would itself indicate failure.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Expect agentic portfolios to differ at the margin, not wholesale, under institutional guardrails.

insights.claim: Ang admits he does not know whether agentic asset allocation beats human-based approaches and says it cannot be known until live performance track records exist.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Treat agentic investing claims as unproven until live track records accumulate.
insights.quote: is it better than what we have now for human-based approaches and to be honest I don't know

insights.claim: Ang draws an analogy to electricity and computing: big productivity gains came only after workflows were redesigned (decentralized power in factories, PCs on every desk), and simply swapping AI into existing processes is the 'unimaginative' use.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Firms that redesign investment workflows around agents, not bolt-on automation, should capture the gains.

insights.claim: Ang predicts that at large asset owners the top decision-makers and entry-level analysts will remain, while middle layers must adapt or be consolidated, with humans moving to exception-based oversight governed by documents like the IPS.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Middle-tier investment staff at institutions face the most role disruption from AI.
insights.quote: the top guy or the top committee and the, you know, entering uh analysts, they're going to be the same

insights.claim: Ang's factor framework diversifies at three layers: multiple signals per factor, multiple factors in the portfolio, and multiple models for tilting factors over time.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Diversify the signal, the factor, and the timing model, not just holdings.

insights.claim: Value's 2018-2020 drawdown was, per Ang, the worst value drawdown in over a century of data before it rebounded from late 2020 into 2021, illustrating the danger of single-factor exposure.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Single-factor bets can endure century-scale drawdowns; combine factors.

insights.claim: Ang splits value into 'enhanced value' (intangible capital and economic value added, i.e. returns above cost of capital) and 'cyclical value' (book-to-market, earnings yield), saying the two are fairly lowly correlated and deserve separate allocations.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Accounting-based value misses intangibles; intangible-adjusted value is a distinct diversifying factor.

insights.claim: Ang's composite momentum factor goes beyond price to include fundamental momentum (analyst revisions), economic-profit momentum, idiosyncratic momentum, low short interest, and hedge fund holdings.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Holdings-based signals like low short interest and hedge fund ownership add predictive power to momentum.

insights.claim: Factor tilts are timed with three models: a market-similarity model weighting past episodes resembling today, factor momentum ('momentum of momentum'), and factor dispersion, where wide valuation spreads make value more attractive and wide winner-loser return spreads favor momentum.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Current valuation and return dispersion across factors are usable timing signals, applied with small active risk.

insights.claim: Ang's core long-run weights are 1/3 momentum, 1/3 quality, 1/6 enhanced value and 1/6 cyclical value, with size and low volatility excluded because their betas diverge from one, making them unsuitable for a low-tracking-error core.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Low-tracking-error factor cores exclude beta-distorting factors such as size and low vol.

insights.claim: The SEI-managed ETF with ticker ANGU (about half a billion dollars in assets per Faber) implements Ang's four-factor, low-tracking-error approach with slight time-varying factor tilts.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A live, investable implementation of the multi-layer factor framework exists.

themes.theme: Uncle Sam's cut: tax drag on equities

insights.claim: Ang's paper 'Uncle Sam's Cut' finds federal taxes dragged US equity returns by roughly 160-170 bps per year over the last 30 years, compounding to about 36% (roughly one-third) of a taxable portfolio, before state and estate taxes.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Tax drag is one of the largest controllable costs for taxable equity investors.
insights.quote: you compound that over 30 years and that results in 30 36% of your portfolio that just disappears

insights.claim: Over the full century 1926-2025 the federal tax drag on US equities averaged about 350 bps per year, peaking above 500 bps in the 1940s-1950s, so the last 30 years' ~165 bps is an anomalously low era rather than the norm.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: If tax regimes mean-revert, after-tax equity returns could fall materially from recent experience.
insights.quote: this kind of modern era, it's it's the anomaly, right? It's not the norm

insights.claim: Dividend taxes have historically contributed most of Uncle Sam's cut, but their share has shrunk because dividend yields fell from about 4-5% in the early 20th century to 1-2% today and qualified dividends moved to the 23.8% capital-gains rate.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Lower payouts and preferential rates are why today's tax drag is historically low.

insights.claim: Taxing dividends and interest every year interrupts tax-deferred compounding permanently, which is why a small annual drag compounds into a third of the portfolio; Faber cites Warren Buffett's no-dividend Berkshire as the exemplar of exploiting this.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Favor deferral (retained earnings, unrealized gains) over distributions in taxable accounts.

insights.claim: Ang says the top combined marginal rate for a New York City resident is 55.576%, stacking federal, New York State 10.9% and NYC 3.876%, versus California's 13.3% state top rate.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: High-tax-jurisdiction investors face far larger after-tax gaps than federal-only studies show.
insights.quote: The highest marginal rate for someone in New York City is 55.576%

themes.theme: After-tax view of yield products and private credit

insights.claim: Because private credit yields are fully taxed as ordinary income, including payment-in-kind, a 10% private credit yield is worth roughly 7% in equity-equivalent after-tax terms, and private credit needs about 14-15% yield to match a 10% equity return.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Pre-tax private credit yields overstate their appeal to taxable investors versus equities.
insights.quote: what's the return in private credit that's needed to match your, you know, 10% in in equity, you need like 14 15% uh yield there

insights.claim: Ang argues many popular option-based or engineered 'income-enhanced' yield products are generally taxed as income and are inferior to investors simply selling appreciated stock themselves.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Taxable investors should be skeptical of yield-engineered ETFs and products.
insights.quote: You're you're you're much better off um selling off appreciated stock on your own

insights.claim: Faber and Ang agree that tax alpha is vastly easier to capture than investment alpha, though investors spend 95-99% of their attention on investment selection.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Tax-aware implementation is a more reliable edge than security selection for most investors.
insights.quote: It's vastly easier in my mind to get alpha from taxes than it is from investments.

themes.theme: Rising taxes, asset location and the post-2% inflation world

insights.claim: Ang expects US taxes to rise, citing debt-to-GDP above 100% (World War II levels) and interest payments consuming about 15% of the federal budget, more than defense spending.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Plan portfolios for higher future tax rates on investment income.
insights.quote: I think taxes are going up.

insights.claim: Ang's asset-location framework at Tao Balance models every asset in every account (taxable, Roth, IRA, 401k, trusts, corporations), since differing after-tax cash flows imply different optimal holdings per account, solved as a multi-period problem tied to explicit objectives.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Holistic multi-account, multi-period optimization is where tax alpha is generated.

insights.claim: Equities in taxable accounts are attractive for bequest goals because of the step-up in basis at death, while for retirement saving the tax-advantaged growth in 401(k)s and IRAs is more valuable.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Asset location should depend on whether wealth is for heirs or for retirement spending.

insights.claim: The academic literature is split on whether taxes are priced in equity valuations because it depends on whether the marginal investor is a tax-exempt sovereign wealth fund or a taxable wealthy individual, though higher tax uncertainty does command a risk premium.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Rising tax uncertainty, not just tax levels, could pressure valuations.

insights.claim: Ang says the world is not going back to 2% inflation, which challenges the bond-heavy strategies that worked for 30 years and calls for new fixed-income levers such as bond tax-loss harvesting and restructured payoffs taxed more favorably than ordinary income.
insights.speaker: Andrew Ang
insights.so_what: Bond allocations need redesign for higher inflation and tax efficiency.
insights.quote: we're kind of not going back I think to a 2% inflation world
